transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Ms. Tremblay, thank you for meeting with me. I have Dr. Miller here with me. I need to discuss what happened with your medication this morning.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want to know why my skin is still itching and why I had to get those shots.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am very sorry. I made a mistake. Your chart clearly lists an allergy to Ceftriaxone, but I overlooked that when I wrote the prescription. I prescribed the drug you are allergic to, and that is why you had the reaction.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So you didn't check the chart.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, I did not check the allergy list before ordering the medication. That is entirely my fault. I apologize for putting you at risk.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It was a pretty intense reaction. I felt like my throat was closing for a second.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't really care about the apology. I just need to know if this is going to affect my medical clearance for deployment.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Let's look at the clinical side of things. The anaphylactoid response was managed with epinephrine and steroids. Since you've responded well to the rescue meds, your vitals are stable. We just need to monitor for a biphasic reaction, which is when symptoms return after the initial treatment.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What does that mean for my timeline?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It means you stay in the hospital for another twenty-four hours for observation.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is a problem. I have a briefing tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know this is frustrating, but—

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It's not frustrating, it's an obstacle. Can I just be monitored at home?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, because the biphasic response can be sudden. I have to make sure you are safe here.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is a waste of a day.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. I'll check your blood pressure now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Why did this happen if it's written in the chart? Is the software broken?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The software is working. I simply missed the alert. It was a failure in my process. I am the one responsible for this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Fine. Whatever. So what happens now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The plan is that we keep you on a baseline of antihistamines for the next twelve hours. I will personally review every single order for your care for the remainder of your stay to ensure there are no further errors.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And when do I get out?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: If your vitals remain stable and there are no new hives, you will be discharged at 10:00 AM tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I need a written report of the incident for my commanding officer.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will have a formal incident report drafted by 5:00 PM today. I will print a copy for you to take, and I can also send a digital copy to your military health liaison if you provide the contact info.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'll give you the email.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Thank you. I also want to tell you that I've already flagged this with our pharmacy lead to see if we can implement a secondary hard-stop in the system for high-risk allergies.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That sounds like a good use of the mistake.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I agree. Is there anything else about the reaction or the timeline you want to clarify?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No. Just get the paperwork done.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll get started on that now. I'll be back in an hour to check your lungs.

H.justification: Resident never interrupts the patient and remains regulated and professional despite the patient's frustration and dismissiveness.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the second turn using lay language, but there were no explicit comprehension checks (e.g., 'Does that make sense?').

A.justification: Resident used direct apology language ('I am very sorry', 'I apologize') and took full personal responsibility without deflection, even when the patient asked if the software was broken.

R.justification: Resident used generic validation ('I understand') twice but did not name specific emotions or engage deeply with the patient's emotional bids.

T.justification: Resident provided specific next steps with timelines (discharge at 10:00 AM, report by 5:00 PM) and addressed prevention, but did not define a specific role for the patient in the plan.
